passage: I'm Tushar, and I first really noticed my mother, Ganga, when I was fifteen and found her at midnight hemming other people's blouses again. She'd done it for years so I could stay in school, and I'd never once asked how her shoulders felt. That night I said thank you, badly, and she waved it away. I felt warm and heavy at once. I told myself I would become an engineer, earn a lot, and pay it all back. Then one evening, sketching buildings in my notebook, I realised I didn't want to be an engineer; I wanted to be an architect. When I said so, she stopped sewing. "I didn't work for your life to belong to me," she said. Now I cook dinner twice a week and keep drawing.

qa.q: What was Ganga doing at midnight when Tushar noticed her?
What two feelings did Tushar have after thanking Ganga?
qa.a: Warmth and heaviness, meaning gratitude together with the pressure to succeed and repay her.

qa.q: What did Tushar do that was fair to Ganga and to Tushar too?
qa.a: Tushar said thanks and took on a real responsibility by cooking dinner twice a week, but kept drawing instead of giving up the architect dream to repay her.

qa.q: How does Ganga see what she has done for Tushar?
qa.a: As a gift, not a debt. She stopped sewing and said she didn't work for Tushar's life to belong to her.

grounding: Tushar sees a parent's sacrifices with gratitude and pressure, thanks her, shares responsibility and keeps a personal dream.
